1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	Several limitations constrain the generalizability of our findings.
5	
6	\paragraph{Model scale.}
7	Our experiments are validated at scales ${\leq}1.4$B parameters (GPT-2-medium 345M, Pythia-410M, OPT-1.3B), all decoder-only transformers small by contemporary standards.
8	Whether the temporal lead shortens or vanishes at frontier scale (7B+) is an open question requiring proportionally more compute per condition: 10 generations $\times$ 5{,}000 steps per generation makes iterative training at 7B+ prohibitively expensive for academic settings.
9	Encoder-decoder architectures (T5, BART) and non-autoregressive models (e.g., diffusion-based text generators) are entirely untested; their fundamentally different generation mechanisms may alter canary dynamics in ways that autoregressive decoder-only results cannot predict.
10	The batch size difference between architectures (4 for Pythia vs.\ 32 for GPT-2-medium) means each training step exposes $8\times$ more data in the latter, potentially accelerating collapse dynamics without altering the qualitative pattern.
11	
12	\paragraph{Data domain and scale.}
13	Training data is drawn from a 5K-document subset of WikiText-103, three orders of magnitude smaller than typical pre-training corpora.
14	This scale gap means our iterative training dynamics reflect a low-data regime where overfitting to synthetic content may onset faster than in production-scale pipelines.
15	Domain-specific properties (vocabulary richness, syntactic complexity, topical diversity) may further influence canary-downstream coupling, and domains with inherently low diversity (e.g., legal text, code) could exhibit different canary dynamics.
16	The C4-domain generalization experiments (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) introduce an additional confound: switching from WikiText to C4 simultaneously changes both the textual domain and the data-scale characteristics, preventing full disentanglement of domain effects from scale effects within a single experimental comparison.
17	
18	\paragraph{Pre-training data confound (C4).}
19	Our C4-domain generalization experiments (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) use Pythia models that were pre-trained on the Pile~\cite{gao2021pile}, which includes Common Crawl data overlapping with C4.
20	This means the model has prior exposure to the domain used for iterative training, potentially conflating domain familiarity with collapse dynamics.
21	The WikiText-103 experiments do not share this confound because Pythia's pre-training corpus does not include WikiText-103 directly.
22	Interpreting C4 results therefore requires caution: observed differences from the WikiText baseline may reflect domain familiarity effects rather than genuine domain-dependent collapse behavior.
23	
24	\paragraph{Short time series ($T{=}10$).}
25	With 11 data points per series, our statistical analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
26	This limits power for all methods and renders two of the five evaluated methods effectively inoperative: threshold onset detection yields 0/8 significant pairs in the majority of conditions under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power relative to the primary methods (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
27	Both threshold onset and Toda--Yamamoto are classified as supplementary: the former due to power limitations (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}), the latter due to sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ and lower detection rates at $T{=}11$; longer generation chains ($T{\geq}20$) could improve both methods' power.
28	Our method recommendation (permutation Granger) is robust at $T{=}10$; threshold onset could become viable at $T{\geq}20$ with additional degrees of freedom.
29	We omit transfer entropy, a standard nonlinear Granger alternative, because kernel density estimation requires substantially longer time series (typically $T{\geq}100$) than our 10-generation design permits, yielding negligible statistical power at $T{=}10$.
30	Longer generation chains would improve statistical power but impose substantial computational cost.
31	
32	\paragraph{Bivariate Granger $\neq$ causality.}
33	Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders.
34	An unobserved process (such as a latent shift in the training data distribution) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations.
35	Our multi-method consensus framework mitigates but does not eliminate this limitation; multivariate VAR models would be required to test for confounders directly.
36	
37	\paragraph{Regime boundary uncertainty.}
38	The onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$ has been refined by probing at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$ (all 0/8), narrowing the transition to a ${\leq}0.05$-wide interval; a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (FDR $p{=}0.053$) but does not reach aggregate detection.
39	Whether this boundary is sharp (phase-transition-like) or gradual, and whether it shifts with model scale or data properties, remains open.
40	Three-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.75$ on WikiText confirms directional asymmetry (20/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), leaving the exact boundary position uncertain.
41	Directional asymmetry itself is domain-dependent: C4 exhibits near-symmetric bidirectional coupling at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (PermG reverse 7/8; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and whether this pattern generalizes to other domains or contamination levels is untested.
42	The canary blind spot observed at $\alpha{=}0.10$ (diversity collapsed but canary silent) rests on a single seed; multi-seed confirmation is needed to establish whether this dissociation is robust.
43	
44	\paragraph{Intervention scope.}
45	Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}) validate canary-based predictive cessation across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, but only at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (full synthetic replacement).
46	Whether the 15\% entropy threshold remains effective under partial contamination or accumulate-mode training is untested; the $\alpha{=}0.60$ trigger observation (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) remains without intervention validation.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Several limitations constrain the generalizability of our findings.

\paragraph{Model scale.}
Our experiments are validated at scales ${\leq}1.4$B parameters (GPT-2-medium 345M, Pythia-410M, OPT-1.3B), all decoder-only transformers small by contemporary standards.
Whether the temporal lead shortens or vanishes at frontier scale (7B+) is an open question requiring proportionally more compute per condition: 10 generations $\times$ 5{,}000 steps per generation makes iterative training at 7B+ prohibitively expensive for academic settings.
Encoder-decoder architectures (T5, BART) and non-autoregressive models (e.g., diffusion-based text generators) are entirely untested; their fundamentally different generation mechanisms may alter canary dynamics in ways that autoregressive decoder-only results cannot predict.
The batch size difference between architectures (4 for Pythia vs.\ 32 for GPT-2-medium) means each training step exposes $8\times$ more data in the latter, potentially accelerating collapse dynamics without altering the qualitative pattern.

\paragraph{Data domain and scale.}
Training data is drawn from a 5K-document subset of WikiText-103, three orders of magnitude smaller than typical pre-training corpora.
This scale gap means our iterative training dynamics reflect a low-data regime where overfitting to synthetic content may onset faster than in production-scale pipelines.
Domain-specific properties (vocabulary richness, syntactic complexity, topical diversity) may further influence canary-downstream coupling, and domains with inherently low diversity (e.g., legal text, code) could exhibit different canary dynamics.
The C4-domain generalization experiments (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) introduce an additional confound: switching from WikiText to C4 simultaneously changes both the textual domain and the data-scale characteristics, preventing full disentanglement of domain effects from scale effects within a single experimental comparison.

\paragraph{Pre-training data confound (C4).}
Our C4-domain generalization experiments (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) use Pythia models that were pre-trained on the Pile~\cite{gao2021pile}, which includes Common Crawl data overlapping with C4.
This means the model has prior exposure to the domain used for iterative training, potentially conflating domain familiarity with collapse dynamics.
The WikiText-103 experiments do not share this confound because Pythia's pre-training corpus does not include WikiText-103 directly.
Interpreting C4 results therefore requires caution: observed differences from the WikiText baseline may reflect domain familiarity effects rather than genuine domain-dependent collapse behavior.

\paragraph{Short time series ($T{=}10$).}
With 11 data points per series, our statistical analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This limits power for all methods and renders two of the five evaluated methods effectively inoperative: threshold onset detection yields 0/8 significant pairs in the majority of conditions under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power relative to the primary methods (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Both threshold onset and Toda--Yamamoto are classified as supplementary: the former due to power limitations (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}), the latter due to sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ and lower detection rates at $T{=}11$; longer generation chains ($T{\geq}20$) could improve both methods' power.
Our method recommendation (permutation Granger) is robust at $T{=}10$; threshold onset could become viable at $T{\geq}20$ with additional degrees of freedom.
We omit transfer entropy, a standard nonlinear Granger alternative, because kernel density estimation requires substantially longer time series (typically $T{\geq}100$) than our 10-generation design permits, yielding negligible statistical power at $T{=}10$.
Longer generation chains would improve statistical power but impose substantial computational cost.

\paragraph{Bivariate Granger $\neq$ causality.}
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders.
An unobserved process (such as a latent shift in the training data distribution) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations.
Our multi-method consensus framework mitigates but does not eliminate this limitation; multivariate VAR models would be required to test for confounders directly.

\paragraph{Regime boundary uncertainty.}
The onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$ has been refined by probing at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$ (all 0/8), narrowing the transition to a ${\leq}0.05$-wide interval; a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (FDR $p{=}0.053$) but does not reach aggregate detection.
Whether this boundary is sharp (phase-transition-like) or gradual, and whether it shifts with model scale or data properties, remains open.
Three-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.75$ on WikiText confirms directional asymmetry (20/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), leaving the exact boundary position uncertain.
Directional asymmetry itself is domain-dependent: C4 exhibits near-symmetric bidirectional coupling at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (PermG reverse 7/8; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and whether this pattern generalizes to other domains or contamination levels is untested.
The canary blind spot observed at $\alpha{=}0.10$ (diversity collapsed but canary silent) rests on a single seed; multi-seed confirmation is needed to establish whether this dissociation is robust.

\paragraph{Intervention scope.}
Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}) validate canary-based predictive cessation across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, but only at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (full synthetic replacement).
Whether the 15\% entropy threshold remains effective under partial contamination or accumulate-mode training is untested; the $\alpha{=}0.60$ trigger observation (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) remains without intervention validation.

\paragraph{Replace-only protocol.}
Our experiments use replace-only data accumulation; accumulate-mode training~\cite{dey2024breaking,kazdan2025collapse} may exhibit qualitatively different canary dynamics or eliminate the need for canary monitoring entirely~\cite{falahati2026curated}.

\paragraph{Scope limited to diversity metrics.}
Our canary claims are scoped to distinct-$n$ diversity metrics~\cite{li2016diversity}, not to model collapse broadly~\cite{schaeffer2025position}, as the perplexity channel proved spurious after differencing.
This scoping is theoretically motivated by the calibration-diversity tradeoff~\cite{cao2025entropycal}, but means our findings may not generalize to other collapse manifestations (e.g., factual degradation, reasoning capability loss).
